es.summary: Alteración precancerosa del epitelio esofágico, generalmente asociada a reflujo gastroesofágico crónico y Barrett.
key_points: Daño crónico por GERD lleva a metaplasia y luego a displasia.
Principal factor de riesgo: esófago de Barrett.
Se diagnostica con endoscopia y biopsia dirigida.
Tratamiento incluye inhibidores de bomba de protones y vigilancia endoscópica.
Complicación principal es el adenocarcinoma esofágico.

pathophysiology: Reflujo ácido causa lesión repetida del epitelio escamoso.
Proceso de reparación induce metaplasia columnar (Barrett).
Daño continuo genera alteraciones genéticas y displasia.
Displasia puede progresar a carcinoma invasivo.
risk_factors: Obesidad y dieta alta en grasas.
Edad > 50 años y antecedentes familiares de cáncer esofágico.
signs_symptoms: Disfagia progresiva a sólidos y luego a líquidos.
Dolor retroesternal o ardor que no mejora con antiácidos.
diagnostics: Endoscopia alta con biopsia dirigida: células displásicas.
pH‑metría esofágica para cuantificar exposición ácida.
Esofagograma de bario para detectar estenosis.
Laboratorio: hemograma completo y perfil nutricional.
treatment: Inhibidores de bomba de protones (omeprazol, pantoprazol).
Modificaciones dietéticas: evitar alimentos irritantes, comidas copiosas.
Elevación de cabecera 30‑45° después de comer.
Vigilancia endoscópica cada 6‑12 meses según grado de displasia.
Resección endoscópica o cirugía en displasia de alto grado.
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor y dificultad para tragar en cada turno.
Monitorear ingesta de líquidos y alimentos; registrar volumen.
Observar signos de aspiración: tos, sibilancias, saturación < 95%.
Mantener cabeza elevada 30‑45° durante y 30 min después de la alimentación.
Administrar PPI según prescripción y registrar efectos.
Preparar al paciente para endoscopia: ayuno y consentimiento.
patient_teaching: Tomar el inhibidor de bomba de protones 30 min antes del desayuno.
Evitar alimentos picantes, cítricos, chocolate y cafeína.
Comer porciones pequeñas y masticar bien los alimentos.
No acostarse durante al menos 2‑3 h después de comer.
Reportar sangrado, pérdida de peso rápida o dificultad creciente para tragar.

outcomes: Seguridad de la vía aérea: sin episodios de aspiración en 48 h
Oxigenación adecuada: saturación de O2 ≥ 95% en reposo

interventions.action: Mantener la cabeza del paciente elevada 30‑45° durante y después de la alimentación.
interventions.rationale: Reduce el riesgo de reflujo y aspiración de contenido gástrico.

interventions.action: Evaluar la capacidad de deglución antes de cada comida.
interventions.rationale: Identifica deterioro que pueda predisponer a aspiración.

interventions.action: Administrar PPI según indicación y observar respuesta clínica.
interventions.rationale: Controla la acidez y disminuye irritación que favorece el reflujo.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de deglución segura y evitar líquidos muy calientes o fríos.
interventions.rationale: Mejora la coordinación de la deglución y reduce el riesgo de ingreso de contenido a la vía aérea.

interventions.action: Monitorear signos de aspiración (tos, sibilancias, cambios en la saturación).
interventions.rationale: Permite intervención temprana ante eventos de aspiración.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos
outcomes: Hidratación adecuada: ingesta de líquidos ≥ 1500 mL/día
Peso estable: variación < 0.5 kg en 48 h

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos cada turno.
interventions.rationale: Permite detectar déficit de volumen temprano.

interventions.action: Ofrecer líquidos en pequeñas cantidades y frecuentemente.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la tolerancia en pacientes con disfagia.

interventions.action: Proveer alimentos blandos y bien hidratados según orden médica.
interventions.rationale: Reduce el esfuerzo de deglución y mejora la ingesta calórica y hídrica.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de deshidratación (turgencia cutánea, mucosas secas, taquicardia).
interventions.rationale: Identifica rápidamente la necesidad de intervención.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente y familia sobre la importancia de mantener hidratación y reconocer signos de deshidratación.
interventions.rationale: Promueve autocuidado y prevención de complicaciones.

en.summary: A precancerous alteration of the esophageal epithelium, usually associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux and Barrett's esophagus.
key_points: Chronic GERD damage leads to metaplasia and then dysplasia.
Diagnosed with endoscopy and targeted biopsy.
Treatment includes proton pump inhibitors and endoscopic surveillance.

pathophysiology: Acid reflux causes repeated injury to the squamous epithelium.
Continuous damage generates genetic alterations and dysplasia.
Dysplasia can progress to invasive carcinoma.
risk_factors: Age > 50 years and family history of esophageal cancer.
signs_symptoms: Progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids.
Retrosternal pain or burning that does not improve with antacids.
diagnostics: High‑resolution endoscopy with targeted biopsy: dysplastic cells.
Esophageal pH monitoring to quantify acid exposure.
Laboratory: complete blood count and nutritional profile.
treatment: Dietary modifications: avoid irritant foods, large meals.
Endoscopic surveillance every 6‑12 months depending on dysplasia grade.
Endoscopic resection or surgery for high‑grade dysplasia.
nursing_care: Assess pain and difficulty swallowing each shift.
Monitor fluid and food intake; record volume.
Observe for aspiration signs: cough, wheeze, SpO₂ < 95%.
Maintain head elevation 30‑45° during and 30 min after feeding.
Administer PPI as prescribed and record effects.
Prepare patient for endoscopy: fasting and consent.
patient_teaching: Take the proton pump inhibitor 30 min before breakfast.
Avoid spicy foods, citrus, chocolate, and caffeine.
Eat small portions and chew food well.
Do not lie down for at least 2‑3 h after eating.
Report bleeding, rapid weight loss, or increasing difficulty swallowing.

outcomes: Airway safety: no aspiration episodes in 48 h

interventions.action: Maintain the patient's head elevated 30‑45° during and after meals.
interventions.rationale: Reduces the risk of reflux and aspiration of gastric contents.

interventions.action: Assess swallowing ability before each meal.
interventions.rationale: Identifies deterioration that may predispose to aspiration.

interventions.action: Administer PPI as indicated and monitor clinical response.
interventions.rationale: Controls acidity and reduces irritation that favors reflux.

interventions.action: Teach the patient safe swallowing techniques and avoid very hot or cold liquids.
interventions.rationale: Improves swallowing coordination and reduces the risk of airway entry.

interventions.action: Monitor for aspiration signs (cough, wheeze, changes in saturation).
interventions.rationale: Allows early intervention for aspiration events.

outcomes: Stable weight: change < 0.5 kg in 48 h

interventions.action: Record fluid intake and output each shift.
interventions.rationale: Detects early volume deficit.

interventions.action: Offer fluids in small amounts frequently.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates tolerance in patients with dysphagia.

interventions.action: Provide soft, well‑hydrated foods as ordered.
interventions.rationale: Reduces swallowing effort and improves caloric and fluid intake.

interventions.action: Assess dehydration signs (skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia).
interventions.rationale: Rapidly identifies need for intervention.

interventions.action: Educate patient and family on the importance of maintaining hydration and recognizing dehydration signs.
interventions.rationale: Promotes self‑care and complication prevention.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: researchers believe that damage to the squamous esophageal cells resulting from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causes the cells to undergo constant repair and wound healing.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Common problems with the esophagus include GI inflammation, esophagitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) , esophageal varices, and hiatal hernia.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: A condition called Barrett’s esophagus entails the cells lining the esophagus change, becoming more like intestinal cells.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Acute gastritis is usually caused by an irritant, such as aspirin or NSAID use, heavy alcohol use, smoking, and certain infections.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: For PUD, life-threatening, or alarm symptoms that warrant immediate action are bleeding or anemia early satiety family history of GI cancers progressive dysphagia or odynophagia recurrent vomiting unexplained weight loss

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: If either of the esophageal sphincters is not functioning properly, ingested food, fluids, and acidic stomach contents may move backward into the esophagus, causing irritation or damage to the tissues.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Other symptoms include heartburn, dyspepsia, chest discomfort, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), melena (black tarry stools), fatigue, and dyspnea

sections.complications.0.quote: The cells that develop on the esophagus can be precancerous and increase the patient’s chance of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma (Souza & Spechler, 2022).

sections.complications.1.quote: In some cases, Barrett’s esophagus can cause ulceration and stricture, and patients may have the symptoms of dysphagia or odynophagia (painful swallowing).

sections.complications.3.quote: Gastritis can be painful and impair digestion and may cause life-threatening complications, such as bleeding or perforation.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: The nurse may ensure the patient receives prescribed proton pump inhibitor s as ordered.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Foods that are spicy, fatty, acidic, or contain caffeine, carbonation, or alcohol can exacerbate symptoms of reflux and heartburn and trigger episodes of odynophagia or dysphagia.
